transcript.text: Dropped a cast iron pan on my ceramic hob and there's a crack right across the front left ring. It still heats up. Can I keep using it until I get a new one?

No — if it’s a true crack in the ceramic glass, stop using the hob, including that ring. A cracked surface can let spills/moisture reach live electrical parts, and heat can make the crack spread or cause the glass to fail suddenly. There’s a risk of electric shock, short-circuiting, or fire even though it still heats normally.

What to do now:

• Switch the hob off at its isolator switch or circuit breaker, not just the touch controls.
• Don’t place pans on the cracked area or pour/clean with liquids around it.
• Arrange repair or replacement through the manufacturer or a qualified appliance engineer. Often the glass top can be replaced, but it depends on model and cost.
• Don’t try to seal it with glue, tape, or a glass repair kit.

If you notice sparking, buzzing, a burning smell, tripped electrics, or the crack worsening, keep it powered off and seek urgent professional help.

A light surface scratch is different, but a crack running across a cooking ring should be treated as unsafe.
Ok, I can switch it off at the red cooker switch on the wall. Some pasta water got spilled earlier and might have gone into the crack, is that a problem?

Yes, that makes it more urgent to leave it switched off. Pasta water is salty, so it can conduct electricity and may also cause corrosion if it has got beneath the glass through the crack.

• Once the hob is cool and your hands are dry, switch it off at the red cooker isolator switch. If you can safely identify the correct circuit at the consumer unit/fuse box, switching that breaker off as well is extra reassurance.
• Do not turn it back on “to see if it’s okay,” even if it appears dry later.
• Don’t pour more water or cleaning fluid onto it, and don’t try to force anything into the crack or seal it.
• Wipe up only the surface spill with a dry/very lightly damp cloth after isolation, avoiding pushing liquid into the crack.

If it trips the electrics, smells burnt, makes a buzzing/crackling sound, or shows any sign of heat while supposedly off, keep clear of it and contact an electrician/appliance engineer. Arrange replacement or a manufacturer-approved repair before using the hob again.
